entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Dedumose II, a pharaoh whose very existence and precise regnal dates remain subjects of scholarly debate, is typically placed within the tumultuous Second Intermediate Period of ancient Egypt, likely around 1600 BCE, a time characterized by political fragmentation and foreign domination. Often associated with the 16th Dynasty of Theban rulers, or possibly a local potentate contemporary with the Hyksos 15th Dynasty, his significance lies in representing the complex and often obscure nature of power dynamics during an era when Egypt was fractured into competing spheres of influence. His name, known primarily from a single stela, reflects the ephemeral authority of numerous minor kings who struggled to maintain control amidst the collapse of the Middle Kingdom and before the re-unification under the New Kingdom.

The core evidence for Dedumose II's reign is a stela from Gebelein, south of Thebes, which names him as a 'King's Son' and 'King.' This artifact suggests a localized assertion of royal authority, potentially over Upper Egypt, during a period when the Hyksos kings (15th Dynasty) controlled the Nile Delta and parts of Middle Egypt from Avaris. While no extensive building projects, military campaigns, or administrative reforms are directly attributed to him, his presence on the stela indicates a continuation of pharaonic titularies and an attempt to legitimize rule within the traditional Egyptian framework, even if his actual power was severely circumscribed by the prevailing geopolitical realities.
